title: Preferred Stimulation Levels in Introverts and Extraverts: Effects on Arousal and Performance

findings.antecedent: Personality type (extravert)
findings.consequent: Chosen noise intensity level (0-100 dial setting)
findings.mechanism: extravert must seek out more intense stimulation to reach the same optimal level of arousal attained by the introvert under less intense conditions
findings.quote: extraverts chose a higher level of intensity for the bursts of noise they received than did introverts. The mean setting¹ for introverts was 37.3, and for extraverts it was 54.2, t(18) = 2.72, p < .01.

findings.antecedent: Treatment condition (choice, assigned-same, assigned-other) or personality (E-I)
findings.quote: No differences were found in PR across either the treatment or personality variables among data from the baseline measure.

findings.antecedent: Condition (choice vs. assigned-same for same personality type)
findings.consequent: Mean pulse rate (PR) during waiting period + Trial 1
findings.mechanism: the mere fact of making a choice did not affect PR
findings.quote: The results indicate that PR in each of the assigned-same conditions did not differ from that in the appropriate choice condition. Thus, the mere fact of making a choice did not affect PR.

findings.antecedent: Personality (introvert vs. extravert) in assigned conditions
findings.consequent: Mean pulse rate (PR) during waiting period + Trial 1
findings.mechanism: introverts are more excitable or arousable than extraverts in response to given levels of stimulation
findings.quote: An analysis of variance (ANOVA) of the data for subjects in the assigned conditions only reveals main effects for both E-I, F(1, 36) = 8.67, p < .01... At both levels of intensity, introverts showed higher pulse rates than extraverts.

findings.antecedent: Any condition or period

findings.antecedent: Condition (choice vs. assigned-same for same personality type)
findings.consequent: Mean trials to criterion (PA learning performance)
findings.quote: the mere fact of choice did not influence performance-subjects who were assigned noise equal in intensity to that chosen by their yoked counterparts in the assigned-same conditions performed as well as the latter.

findings.antecedent: Personality (E-I) x Noise Intensity (introvert-chosen vs. extravert-chosen)
findings.consequent: Mean trials to criterion (PA learning performance)
findings.mechanism: if introverts and extraverts were to attain a comparable level of arousal by selecting levels of stimulation appropriate to each personality, performance on a PA learning task would likewise be comparable across the two groups

findings.quote: extraverts did not differ from introverts when stimulated at a level preferred by introverts.

findings.mechanism: introverts show the higher PR but at the extremes (A and D) the difference becomes nonsignificant
findings.quote: introverts showed higher PR in response to both of the intermediate levels of noise.

findings.mechanism: extraverts stimulated at theoretical level C (the optimal level for extraverts) are equal in PR to introverts stimulated at level B (the optimal level for introverts)
findings.quote: extraverts stimulated at theoretical level C (the optimal level for extraverts) are equal in PR to introverts stimulated at level B (the optimal level for introverts).

findings.mechanism: the most efficient learning took place when the subject was stimulated at some moderate level of intensity

stimuli.description: Recorded white noise delivered in random short bursts (1s duration, 10s mean interval) at varying intensity levels (0-100 dial setting, corresponding to 40-85 dB SPL).

tables.description: Mean Trials to Criterion for Extraverts and Introverts across Choice, Assigned Introvert Choice, and Assigned Extravert Choice noise treatments in Experiment 1.
Mean Trials to Criterion for Extraverts and Introverts across Low, Mod-low, Mod-high, and High noise conditions in Experiment 2.

limitations: Conclusions regarding the effects of deviation from an optimal level of stimulation cannot be drawn with any greater certainty from Experiment 1 (e.g., what would have resulted had introverts been stimulated at a suboptimal level or extraverts at a superoptimal one).

In Experiment 2, due to an apparatus malfunction, conductance data were collected for only slightly more than half the subjects, and blood volume measures were the only psychophysiological data available.
Cue utilization is only one possible explanation for the findings; arousal has also been shown to influence memory through its effects on retrieval and rehearsal of material prior to retrieval.
